{"id": "17:106/q13", "question": "What does “ʿalā mukth” mean?", "turns_on": "Whether mukth describes the manner of reciting each passage or the span between and across successive passages.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q13/p1", "position": "The Prophet should recite slowly, deliberately, clearly and with measured tartīl.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly gloss it as tartīl or unhurried reading. Ṭāwūs says clarity enables understanding; Ibn Zayd cites 73:4, while ʿAṭāʾ contrasts measured recitation with casting words away. Al-Ṭabarī and others link measured articulation to listener comprehension; al-Qurṭubī includes a ban on melody that alters text. Mālik also gives deliberate reading. Al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr relate pace to words settling in hearts."}, {"id": "17:106/q13/p2", "position": "It denotes intervals or a long span over which passages came and were recited.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī distinguishes a pause before another passage descends from Abū Muslim's reciting one portion after another. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān give a long duration; al-Biqāʿī sees each portion read at its own time over twenty-three years. Al-Jishumī and al-Samīn explain makth as pause or long duration; Abū Ḥayyān says long stay."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q14", "question": "How does “ʿalā mukth” attach syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase modifies recitation, the act of division, or the people; the last is rejected on semantic grounds.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q14/p1", "position": "It describes the reader or recitation as a circumstance of the reading.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attaches it to li-taqraʾahu despite repeated ʿalā. Al-Samīn reports an implicit circumstance of reader or text, but objects that a circumstantial analysis needs an implicit governor if described that way. Ālūsī reports Abū al-Baqāʾ's state reading."}, {"id": "17:106/q14/p2", "position": "It attaches directly to faraqnāhu, describing division in stages.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn lists this as a third parse, and Ālūsī notes the disagreement between attachment to faraqnāhu and li-taqraʾahu."}, {"id": "17:106/q14/p3", "position": "It is an apposition to ʿalā al-nās.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥawfī proposes this; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Ālūsī reject it because delay characterizes the reader or recitation, not the people."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q15", "question": "How is the mīm of “mukth” vocalized?", "turns_on": "Claims of consensus on ḍamma coexist with named fatḥa transmissions; the three Arabic vowel patterns do not all have reported Qurʾānic readings.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q15/p1", "position": "Ḍamma is the common or canonical reading.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report it; Ibn ʿAṭiyya claims unanimity, while Qurṭubī excepts Ibn Muḥayṣin and later reports attest fatḥa. Arabic has three noun or verb forms according to al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and al-Jishumī."}, {"id": "17:106/q15/p2", "position": "Fatḥa is a reported reading or dialect form with the same sense.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī names Anas, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda and Abū Rajāʾ; Qurṭubī names Ibn Muḥayṣin. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Wāḥidī compare the verb at 27:22, and al-Rāzī gives both forms. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn and Ālūsī attest it. Kasra is an Arabic form but al-Samīn knows no reading of it."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q16", "question": "What practice follows from measured recitation?", "turns_on": "Whether tartīl is specifically measured delivery or also observance of textual order.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q16/p1", "position": "Deliberate recitation with full articulation and reflection has priority over speed.", "reasons": "Mujāhid prefers al-Baqara recited slowly to a faster greater quantity when other prayer acts are equal; Ibn ʿAbbās prefers slow al-Baqara to a quick full Qurʾān. Ibn Masʿūd advises at least three days and recommends seven. Qurṭubī says melodic alteration of the text is forbidden."}, {"id": "17:106/q16/p2", "position": "Tartīl can mean reciting in the established Qurʾānic order.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports some who condemn reversing order and construe an oath to read in order that way, citing 73:4."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q17", "question": "What does the final “tanzīlan” add?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal noun stresses the actual staged descent or itself denotes clarification.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q17/p1", "position": "The cognate accusative intensifies the assertion of staged descent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it reinforcement of the preceding sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the doubled verb and cognate object signal staged revelation, and argues that the heavier transitive form pragmatically suggests abundance; he reports al-Zamakhsharī's pairing of anzal and nazzala. Al-Rāzī says the final clause restates the described manner and quality."}, {"id": "17:106/q17/p2", "position": "Tanzīl means clarification here.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī gives this gloss."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q18", "question": "Why was the Qurʾān revealed and recited in stages?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary purposes: ease of learning, responses to events, steadiness for the Prophet, gradual uptake of duties, and unity across installments.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q18/p1", "position": "Stages make reception, memorization, understanding and reflection easier.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Study Quran and others give this rationale. Rāzī answers an objection that staged delivery could look like composition by the Messenger; instead it aids memory and grasp of details. Al-Biqāʿī stresses sustained teaching; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī pairs learning with practice. Elmalılı says even a verse may be a complete lesson. Al-Jaʿbarī adds short-sūra milestones and rest."}, {"id": "17:106/q18/p2", "position": "Stages meet new events, questions and people's changing needs.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says verses answered questions and replies to the Prophet. The Qurʾān came day by day as circumstances unfolded. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 25:32 and the demand for one book; al-Suyūṭī reports Ibn ʿAbbās that each new polytheist challenge drew an answer (25:33). Elmalılı describes movement from foundations to subsidiary matters."}, {"id": "17:106/q18/p3", "position": "Stages strengthened the Prophet's heart and renewed divine reassurance.", "reasons": "Al-Durr links the reply to the polytheists' demand at 25:32; Ibn ʿĀshūr supplies this implicit wisdom from measured recitation and 25:32. Al-Biqāʿī says repeated news from the beloved was like a daily celebration. Study Quran says the staged descent was divinely intended."}, {"id": "17:106/q18/p4", "position": "Stages let obligations and social change take hold gradually.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says a simultaneous arrival of all duties would repel people. Al-Burhān says abrogating and abrogated material cannot descend together. Elmalılı and Kuranyolu describe people leaving entrenched beliefs and habits step by step, including wine prohibition."}, {"id": "17:106/q18/p5", "position": "Each passage should still be understood as part of a unified whole.", "reasons": "Asad says gradual revelation does not break the Qurʾān's unity and cites 20:114; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the diverse teachings as issuing from one unified source."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q19", "question": "How does 17:106 connect with its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "How the separated clause relates to the truthful descent, the challenge narrative, and its rhetorical joining.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q19/p1", "position": "It explains the preceding truthful descent and the opponents' demand for a single complete revelation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr coordinates it with 17:105 and points to 25:32 for the omitted wisdom. Al-Durr likewise connects 25:32. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ places it after the sūra's challenge at 17:88 and demands at 17:89–96; 17:105–109 then affirm truthful descent and believers' response. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds the demand of the People of the Book at 4:153."}, {"id": "17:106/q19/p2", "position": "The clause separation has rhetorical force beyond labeling it a fresh start.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī says joining and separating clauses is subtle and merely calling an unjoined clause a new start fails to explain the choice."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q20", "question": "What do the verse's divisions imply about sūras and verses as units?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q20/p1", "position": "A sūra is a bounded, purposefully arranged unit and an āya a distinguishable recitable unit.", "reasons": "Al-Jaʿbarī defines a sūra as an opening and closing around at least three verses; each division is an art and sign, and even al-Kawthar's three verses are miraculous like al-Baqara. He gives teaching, memory, rest and theme as benefits. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī defines verse units by separable recitation, from one word to long passage, and sūras as basmala-prefaced speech organized around a purpose, with reported counting exceptions. Umm Salama's reports of the Prophet pausing at verse ends and traditional counts for al-Fātiḥa and al-Mulk support verse units."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q21", "question": "How is “sūra” derived and used for the Qurʾān's divisions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q21/p1", "position": "It can denote an elevated, ranked or enclosing section of discourse.", "reasons": "Jishumī contrasts unhamzated elevated dwelling with hamzated Qurʾānic section and suʾr, remainder. Al-Qutaybī allows hamza from vessel remainder or an unhamzated sense; others compare building levels, city wall or bracelet enclosure, rank and ordered verses, or elevation and rising (Ibn Jinnī). Al-Burhān distinguishes the plural suwar from the building wall plural and says naming individual sūras is permitted, citing Ibn Masʿūd."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q22", "question": "What is meant by āya, tafsīr and taʾwīl in discussions of the Qurʾān's units?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q22/p1", "position":

"Āya can mean a sign bounding discourse or a group; tafsīr uncovers meaning, while taʾwīl has several accounts.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives āya as a beginning and end marker or collection of letters and reports faʿla/fāʿila analyses; Sībawayh favors medial wāw because that root pattern is common. Abū al-ʿAbbās equates tafsīr, taʾwīl and meaning; another account makes tafsīr explanation of obscure wording and taʾwīl a choice fitting apparent sense; a third derives taʾwīl from final outcome, citing 7:53."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q23", "question": "What divisions of sūras are reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q23/p1", "position": "The seven long sūras, mathānī, miʾūn and mufassal classify Qurʾānic sections.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports a Prophetic comparison with Torah, Gospel and Psalms. The long sūras run from al-Baqara to al-Tawba, or through Yūsuf. Mathānī may mean sūras over one hundred verses with recurring rulings, or al-Fātiḥa; miʾūn are around one hundred verses; mufassal are short sūras with frequent breaks."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q24", "question": "How fixed are verse and sūra counts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q24/p1", "position": "Verse endpoints and total counts vary across regional traditions and are not fixed by a reliable mutawātir text.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī lists Meccan, two Medinan, Syrian, Basran and Kufan lines of transmission. He says a researcher may weigh contextual evidence where boundaries are unclear. He challenges the Kufan count attributed to ʿAlī against basmala reports and notes 114 sūras in the familiar Uthmanic codex versus Ahl al-Bayt joining Barāʾa to the preceding sūra and pairing al-Ḍuḥā/al-Inshirāḥ and al-Fīl/Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q25", "question": "Who arranged and compiled the Qurʾān's sūras and verses?", "turns_on": "Whether Prophetic instruction established both sūra and verse order or only verse order, leaving sūra arrangement to the Companions.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q25/p1", "position": "The Prophet set the arrangement; Companions collected the written and remembered text without addition or loss.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says material lay on palm stalks, stones and in memories and was gathered before memorizers died; the Companions wrote what they heard. Gabriel showed the Prophet placements, says Ibn al-Anbārī, so changing a sūra's place disrupts order. Al-Sulamī says Zayd witnessed the final review with Gabriel, hence Abū Bakr and ʿUthmān chose him. Present order in the Preserved Tablet and whole descent to the lowest heaven are also adduced."}, {"id": "17:106/q25/p2", "position": "The Prophet fixed verse order, but Companions arranged the sūras.", "reasons": "Ibn Fāris distinguishes the two compilations. Makkī allows Companion judgment in sūra order while attributing placement of basmala to the Prophet. Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr reports differing early codex orders, including ʿAlī's chronological start with Iqraʾ, Ibn Masʿūd's al-Fātiḥa/al-Baqara/al-Nisāʾ, and Ubayy's al-Fātiḥa/al-Nisāʾ."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q26", "question": "How can revelation order and Meccan or Medinan status be established?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q26/p1", "position": "Transmitted chronologies exist but conflict, so contextual and internal evidence is needed.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's sequence from Iqraʾ through early Meccan sūras; Medinan lists differ and may omit al-Fātiḥa because of double revelation. Ibn Ḥaṣṣār counts twenty agreed Medinan and twelve disputed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses the value of order for the prophetic mission but questions conflicting reports. Bint al-Shāṭiʾī places ten letter-opened sūras before al-Qaṣaṣ and al-Isrāʾ fiftieth, in the context of the sign challenge."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q27", "question": "What inward counsel is drawn from the Qurʾān's division and address?", "turns_on": "The counsel addresses different spiritual conditions.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q27/p1", "position": "Holding to the Qurʾān brings nearness and recognition; neglect brings deprivation.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī reports the Najmī interpretations on the Qurʾān's rope and consequences of severing it."}, {"id": "17:106/q27/p2", "position": "The sinful should hope in mercy and the righteous should fear pride in their deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī reports Sulamī, a Ḥāfiẓ verse on mercy for a sinful believer, and another verse warning that ascetic pride fails while humility reaches peace."}]}
{"id": "17:106/q28", "question": "How does furqān relate to this Qurʾānic separation?", "turns_on": "Whether furqān names the act of discrimination or its saving result.", "positions": [{"id": "17:106/q28/p1", "position": "It denotes distinction between truth and falsehood.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this to Ibn al-ʿAbbās, citing 8:29."}, {"id": "17:106/q28/p2", "position": "It can denote salvation or escape.", "reasons": "Jishumī also reports this alternative, citing 8:29."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q01", "question": "What prompted the command to call on Allah or al-Raḥmān?", "turns_on": "The reported hearers and names spoken differ.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q01/p1", "position": "Polytheists heard the Prophet invoke both names and accused him of calling on two gods.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and reports through al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Thaʿlabī and others locate the exchange in Mecca, often at night in prostration; some name Abū Jahl. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the report with Allah and al-Raḥmān because those are the verse's two names. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds this occasion best suited to the wording."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p2", "position": "Jews or other People of the Book asked why the Prophet seldom used al-Raḥmān although Torah used it often.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk supplies the Torah comparison; al-Māwardī names converts including Ibn Salām. Bayḍāwī, reported by al-Ālūsī, prefers this occasion because the reference to beautiful names addresses a perceived ranking; al-Ṭībī distinguishes Jewish preference for one name from pagan objection to combining names."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p3", "position": "The Prophet invoked al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm in prostration; pagans mistook the names for two gods.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's report, as conveyed by al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Jišumī and others, specifies a Meccan night prayer and these two mercy names; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the command also implicitly licenses al-Raḥīm."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p4", "position": "A hearer associated al-Raḥmān with Musaylima or another man of Yamāma.", "reasons": "Makḥūl's reports, as cited by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī, name a man in Yamāma; Ibn ʿAbbās reports in al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī name Musaylima. Al-Bursawī relays al-Suhaylī's claim that Musaylima adopted the title before the Prophet's father's birth and was killed by Waḥshī."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p5", "position": "Arabs questioned al-Raḥmān after the Prophet began writing the full basmala.", "reasons": "Maymūn b. Mihrān says the Prophet changed from 'In Your name, O God' to the basmala after 27:30; some reports say Quraysh knew al-Raḥīm but not al-Raḥmān."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p6", "position": "Opponents treated the name al-Raḥmān as evidence of outside religious influence.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says both names were known to Arabs, with Raḥmān perhaps more common among the People of the Book; Quraysh alleged Jewish assistance in making the Qurʾān (25:4) and feared imposition of their tradition. Kur'an Yolu judges concern over use of such names likelier than a two-god rumor; Ibn al-ʿArabī in al-Burhān reads 'what is al-Raḥmān?' (25:60) as ignorance of an attribute, not the name."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p7", "position": "A hearer associated al-Raḥmān with a man in Yemen.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī's Makḥūl report locates the man in Yemen after the Prophet invoked al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm in Meccan night prostration."}, {"id": "17:110/q01/p8", "position": "Jews questioned the name while the Prophet stood in a field with a palm branch.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī's account in al-Durr adds the field, palm branch, Jewish questioners and a priest in Yamāma bearing the title."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q02", "question": "How does the naming command connect to its context?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q02/p1", "position": "It answers surrounding challenges and summons readers to the Qurʾān's revealer.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says opponents, unable to answer the Qurʾān's challenge, accused the Prophet of the plurality he condemned. Al-Biqāʿī ties the command to learned believers' response, repeated mercy language across sūra 17 and prostration; the names meet the imagined question which name to use. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the prior verse occasioned the objection."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q03", "question": "What does 'call upon' mean in the opening command?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is naming with an omitted object or direct invocation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q03/p1", "position": "Name God Allah or al-Raḥmān, with an understood object of the naming verb.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī argues that ayyan requires two alternative designations of one object and reconstructs 'call Him Allah or call Him al-Raḥmān'; al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī say a second object is omitted. Abū Ḥayyān records a construction with bāʾ and a poetic parallel. Ibn Hishām's distinction, cited in al-Itqān, separates genuine ellipsis from a verb used without an intended object; misunderstanding the ellipsis could imply shirk."}, {"id": "17:110/q03/p2", "position": "Invoke God vocatively by either name.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān finds this suited to the occasion reports and distinguishes God's name from His attribute; al-Ālūsī reports and favors his reading against al-Zamakhsharī, while allowing the two designations to be coordinated because their concepts differ. Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Itqān leave both invocation and naming possible."}, {"id": "17:110/q03/p3", "position": "Worship God under either name.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī

notes duʿāʾ can mean worship, adducing 6:71, 10:106, 26:213 and 28:88."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q04", "question": "How is idʿū read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q04/p1", "position": "Readers vary the linking vowels without changing the meaning.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports disagreement among Abū ʿAmr transmitters over lām and wāw, while ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza use kasra on both; Ibn Khālawayh gives ḍamma or kasra on idʿū. Qirāʾāt Er identifies the final lām and another vowel as phonetic liaison."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q05", "question": "What related practices of supplication are reported?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted practices guide petition.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q05/p1", "position": "Call with certainty, attention and requests worthy of divine power; use prophetic prayers.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī transmits Abū Hurayra reports urging certainty of response, an attentive heart and large petitions, naming al-Tirmidhī, al-Ḥākim, Muslim and others as transmitters; at Qurʾān completion he prefers the Prophet's comprehensive supplications over private fixed formulas. Al-Biqāʿī cites the servant's nearness in prostration."}, {"id": "17:110/q05/p2", "position": "Raise the palms for supplication and wipe the face afterward.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī cites Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sāʾib and ʿUmar through Abū Dāwūd, al-Ḥākim and al-Tirmidhī, and adds a personal vision in 792 AH; he says Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām's rejection may reflect not seeing these reports."}, {"id": "17:110/q05/p3", "position": "Wiping the face after supplication is rejected.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām rejects the practice in his fatwas; Ibn al-Jazarī counters that he may not have seen the reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sāʾib and ʿUmar."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q06", "question": "What do the two divine names imply about the One invoked?", "turns_on": "Whether the names are equivalent in reference, efficacy, or rank.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q06/p1", "position": "Both names designate the one God, so either may be used without multiplying deities.", "reasons": "Muqātil points also to the names in 59:24; al-Zajjāj says al-Raḥmān occurs in earlier revelation; Mujāhid extends the permission to every divine name. Al-Biqāʿī distinguishes Allah's majesty from al-Raḥmān's beneficence. Bayḍāwī prefers equal goodness and efficacy in invocation while also reporting equality of referent. Al-Ālūsī relates the answer to 17:111's denial of partner; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses that names guide worship toward their single bearer."}, {"id": "17:110/q06/p2", "position": "The names are equally good or efficacious in invocation, even if their aspects differ.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī prefers equal success in attaining the supplicant's aim because the clause names all of God's beautiful names; al-Ālūsī connects this with the Jewish preference for Raḥmān and relays the view that one good name suffices against it."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q07", "question": "What distinguishes al-Raḥmān and Allah as names?", "turns_on": "Whether al-Raḥmān is a proper name, attribute, or uniquely universal mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q07/p1", "position": "Al-Raḥmān is uniquely divine and denotes encompassing mercy, while Allah gathers divine majesty or the essence.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports al-Ḥasan's exclusivity claim; al-Burhān notes faʿlān is more emphatic than faʿīl and records Ibn Mālik's answer to a poet's indefinite raḥmānan: the poet meant mercy, not the established proper name. Al-Ḥarālī contrasts al-Raḥmān's encompassing creative mercy with al-Raḥīm's particular mercy. Asad calls the grace unconditional; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī derives Allah from al-ilāh, 'worshipped'."}, {"id": "17:110/q07/p2", "position": "Al-Raḥmān chiefly connotes mighty, just kingship rather than mercy alone.", "reasons": "Al-Barzabādhānī in al-Burhān adduces 25:26, 25:60, 19:18, 19:92, 20:108, 21:42 and 19:93 for majesty, power, protection, self-sufficiency and universal sovereignty."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q08", "question": "Which divine names are ranked greatest or preferred?", "turns_on": "What property or word order establishes precedence.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q08/p1", "position": "Allah ranks highest; al-Raḥmān is near it.", "reasons": "Al-Ghazālī says Allah uniquely denotes the essence containing every attribute while other names usually denote single qualities; Raḥmān is also exclusive to God but derives from mercy. Al-Rāzī says these two surpass other names and the order puts Allah first; al-Ālūsī notes that this can address the Jewish ranking claim."}, {"id": "17:110/q08/p2", "position": "Some Jews regarded al-Raḥmān as most beloved or greatest.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī infers this from the Torah's frequent use of the name and allows that Muslims too distinguish ranks among names."}, {"id": "17:110/q08/p3", "position": "The greatest name is implicated in invoking the One, Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is begotten.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites a Prophetic report promising response to a man who invoked God by that formula."}, {"id": "17:110/q08/p4", "position": "The greatest name appears in 2:163 and in the opening of Āl ʿImrān.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites a Prophetic report joining the One Merciful in 2:163 with the Living, Sustaining in 3:1–2."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q09", "question": "How does 'or' relate the two invocations?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse merely permits alternatives or also explicitly permits combining them.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q09/p1", "position": "It offers a choice between two equally valid names.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī read aw as choice; al-Ṭībī in al-Ālūsī says this particularly suits the Jewish objection to preferring one name. {"id": "17:110/q10", "question": "How does 'ayyan mā tadʿū' work?", "turns_on": "Whether the following mā is syntactically extra, emphatic, or another condition.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q10/p1", "position": "Mā is an added or emphatic particle; the conditional answer is introduced by fāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba compare 23:40; al-Wāḥidī also cites 38:11 and 71:25. Al-Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī say tanwīn replaces the genitive complement and mā strengthens generality. Al-Burhān favors calling it a connecting particle because no Qurʾānic particle is meaningless; al-Itqān distinguishes emphatic mā that does and does not cancel governance, with al-Fārisī and Abū al-Baqāʾ emphasizing its force."}, {"id": "17:110/q10/p2", "position": "Ayyan is a conditional object, with an omitted genitive understood; tadʿū is jussive.", "reasons": "Sībawayh treats free ayy like man and illustrates annexed and distributive forms with lines of al-ʿAbbās b. Al-Samīn makes ayyan the object; Ibn ʿĀshūr says mā turns original interrogative ayy conditional."}, {"id": "17:110/q10/p3", "position": "Mā repeats or shares conditional force with ayy.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl's analysis in Sībawayh compares mahmā to two mā particles and the patterns matā mā, in mā and aynamā. {"id": "17:110/q11", "question": "How does 'ayyan mā tadʿū fa-lahu' form its answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q11/p1", "position": "The fāʾ clause supplies, or stands in place of, the conditional answer and refers back to the named God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn rejects an omitted 'it is permissible' followed by a new clause. Al-Ālūsī says the clause supplies the rationale where the consequence is expected, while al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī similarly calls cause substituted for effect; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn reject a pause after ayyan with independent mā because mā cannot denote rational persons and the scope fails. {"id": "17:110/q13", "question": "Where may a reader pause in ayyan mā?", "turns_on": "The relation between the written separate words and syntactic attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q13/p1", "position": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī are reported to stop on ayyan.", "reasons": "Al-Dānī, Ibn Ghalbūn and Ibn Shurayḥ in al-Nashr report this, with disagreement over Ruways; al-Samīn explains that two readers change ayyan's tanwīn to alif at the stop."}, {"id": "17:110/q13/p2", "position": "Other readers stop on mā; some consider this preferable.", "reasons": "Ibn Saʿdān in al-Nashr prefers mā because it augments ayyan; al-Samīn reports the other readers stopping there."}, {"id": "17:110/q13/p3", "position": "Both stopping points are permissible.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī notes most authorities make no special ruling and favors both because the words are separate in the rasm."}]}

{"id": "17:110/q15", "question": "Why are God's names called the Most Beautiful?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q15/p1", "position": "They express divine perfection, praise, holiness, majesty and good attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī lists knowledge, power, hearing, sight, will, speech and life; al-Ṭabrisī groups names of essence, good action and servants' turning to God. {"id": "17:110/q16", "question": "What are divine names in relation to God and spoken words?", "turns_on": "Whether 'name' denotes the divine reality or the human utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q16/p1", "position": "The names' realities point to the divine essence and attributes; spoken labels are created signs distinct from their bearer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes essential positive names, identical with the essence, from actional or negative names that are additional; he calls words names of names. Reports from al-Ṣādiq reject worshipping a name alone or pairing name and meaning as two objects; a report through Ibrāhīm b. ʿUmar describes a hidden name and three manifested parts. {"id": "17:110/q17", "question": "How many divine names are reported?", "turns_on": "Which count and what it promises.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q17/p1", "position": "A report assigns God ninety-nine names.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's report in al-Ṭabarī says these are in the Qurʾān and enumerating them leads to Paradise; Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites the list, and al-Ghazālī in al-Ālūsī compares Allah and Raḥmān among the ninety-nine."}, {"id": "17:110/q17/p2", "position": "A report describes 360 beautiful names derived from twelve pillars, with one hidden name.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits al-Ṣādiq's four pillars each for Allah, Tabārak and Subḥān, thirty names per pillar, with the three revealed forms veiling a hidden name."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q18", "question": "How are divine names established?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q18/p1", "position": "A divine name requires revelation or consensus, not mere rational coinage.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī state this restriction; their concern is that the name truly ascribes a revealed perfection."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q19", "question": "Does the beauty of God's names rule out His creating injustice?", "turns_on": "Whether creating an act makes it an attribute and name of the creator.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q19/p1", "position": "No: creating an act does not make God bear its description.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī replies that creating movement or color does not make God movable or colored; al-Ālūsī likewise denies the inference. Both recommend reverent names such as Creator of heaven and earth or Creator of all instead of distasteful qualified descriptions."}, {"id": "17:110/q19/p2", "position": "Yes: if God created unjust acts, He would acquire an ugly name.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī argues this in al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī, taking the claim that every divine name is beautiful as the premise."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q20", "question": "What does the verse establish about divine action and worship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q20/p1", "position": "It establishes one God to whom petitions are directed and from whom evil or injustice is excluded.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī uses the unity of names and attributes to support invocation by beautiful names before requests and argues that He does no evil or injustice; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says supposed divine offspring and subordinate causes remain servants under God's power."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q21", "question": "How is the voice command read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q21/p1", "position": "A reading attributed to Ibn ʿUmar or ʿAbd Allāh says not to lower or excessively raise 'your voice'.", "reasons": "Abū Razīn's transmission in al-Durr and al-Ālūsī puts the voice explicitly in the wording; al-Durr attributes it to Ibn ʿUmar while al-Ālūsī says ʿAbd Allāh."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q22", "question": "What event prompted the voice command?", "turns_on": "The exact danger and stage of Meccan public recitation.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q22/p1", "position": "Loud Meccan recitation drew pagan abuse, so the Prophet was told to use a volume companions could hear safely.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's report is transmitted by Bukhārī and Muslim per al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī; the abusers reviled the Qurʾān, its revealer and messenger. Saʿīd says Quraysh feared harm to their idols and threatened to curse God; Qatāda mentions abuse and ʿAbd al-Razzāq's report says filth was thrown. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this chain and contextual fit; al-Suyūṭī and al-Nawawī prefer its stronger chain. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites a report that volume exposed the Prophet's location."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p2", "position": "Abū Bakr prayed very quietly and ʿUmar loudly, and each was told to move toward the middle.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr wished to speak privately with God, who knew his need; ʿUmar sought to repel Satan and wake sleepers. Reports through Zayd b. Aslam, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ give the exchange, sometimes with Bilāl changing surahs; some say both practices were first approved."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p3", "position": "Bedouins of Banū Tamīm loudly asked for camels, wealth or children after the Prophet's prayer.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh b. Shaddād's reports differ between asking God and asking the Prophet, and mention the prayer's salutation; the volume of requests prompted the verse."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p4", "position": "A Bedouin or Arab loudly recited the tashahhud.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha and Ibn Sīrīn reports connect the verse to a loudly spoken testimony; al-Suyūṭī says this may clarify ʿĀʾisha's broader supplication report."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p5", "position": "At dawn near al-Ṣafā, Abū Jahl threatened or mocked the Prophet's recitation.", "reasons": "Muqātil places the prayer near Abū Sufyān's house; Abū Jahl objected, then boasted of silencing the Prophet after he lowered his voice. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Jišumī and Ibn al-Jawzī repeat this location and taunt."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p6", "position": "The Prophet's audible basmala mentioning al-Raḥmān drew mockery.", "reasons": "Saʿīd's reports in al-Durr and al-Ālūsī mention association with Musaylima and clapping, gestures or whistling; al-Ālūsī says this fits the preceding naming command. Iṣlāḥī instead suggests pagan noisy worship made quiet Muslim prayer itself an object of complaint."}, {"id": "17:110/q22/p7", "position": "Loud recitation drove listeners away, but overly quiet recitation deprived covert hearers of benefit.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports in al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Durr give the aim of allowing secret listeners to hear without exposing or repelling them."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q23", "question": "How should prayer volume be moderated?", "turns_on": "Whether each prayer requires a middle volume or prayers are divided by prescribed mode.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q23/p1", "position": "Use an audible middle volume in the relevant prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī and Abū Isḥāq explicitly prefer this contextual reading: companions can hear without hostile pagans hearing. Others use the speaker's own hearing as lower bound (Ibn Masʿūd), or enough audibility for followers; al-Jubbāʾī says too much voice distracts nearby worshippers. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports al-Ṣādiq's large-congregation standard, while al-Bayḍāwī calls moderation beloved. Al-Ālūsī reads 'path' as a way toward a goal."}, {"id": "17:110/q23/p2", "position": "Recite some prayers aloud and others quietly, especially night prayers aloud and daytime prayers softly.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā favors Ibn ʿAbbās's report of prescribed modes; Abū Muslim and Abū Yaʿlā articulate night/day. Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes obligatory established modes from optional prayers. Al-Ālūsī gives Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ as loud; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers collective ṣalāt, with dawn, sunset and night aloud and others quiet, and relates audible and quiet modes to transcendence and nearness. Al-Ṭabarī rejects this as contrary to exegetical consensus."}, {"id": "17:110/q23/p3", "position": "Avoid both extremes associated with earlier scriptural communities' prayer styles.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says People of the Book alternated shouting and whispers too low for a letter to be heard; Gabriel taught the Muslim community its middle way. Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn Kathīr specify followers shouting after leaders; Abū Ḥayyān describes Torah and Gospel worshippers' alternating voice."}, {"id": "17:110/q23/p4", "position": "Avoid shouting from ostentation or provocation and whispering from fear; keep prayer audible to intended hearers.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbāʾī warns of distracting nearby worshippers; al-ʿĀshūr says loud public recitation could harden opponents instead of softening hearts, while excessive secrecy deprives potential converts. Elmalılı sees shouted supplication as disrespectful and unheard whisp

{"id": "17:110/q24", "question": "Was the voice instruction abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether the later remembrance command supersedes the Meccan rule.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q24/p1", "position": "Yes, by the command to remember God inwardly in 7:205.", "reasons": "Some Medinan authorities in ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn ʿAbbās in Ibn al-Jawzī transmit this; Ikrima and al-Ḥasan in al-Ṭabarī link the two verses, as does a report in al-Durr."}, {"id": "17:110/q24/p2", "position": "No; the moderation instruction remains operative.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī doubts abrogation, al-Rāzī rejects the 7:55 proposal, and al-Ālūsī says most commentators maintain continuing force."}, {"id": "17:110/q24/p3", "position": "Yes, by the command to proclaim openly in 15:94.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Sāʾib's view is transmitted by Ibn al-Jawzī, who finds abrogation unlikely on closer inspection."}, {"id": "17:110/q24/p4", "position": "Yes, by 7:55's command to call upon God humbly and privately.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports the view in the supplication interpretation; al-Rāzī calls it remote and al-Ālūsī untenable."}, {"id": "17:110/q24/p5", "position": "The Meccan restriction lapsed after the Hijra.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk's report from Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr says the danger ended after migration; al-Durr says the Prophet left that practice then, and al-Ālūsī cites it as a minority abrogation account."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q25", "question": "How does the prayer-volume command connect to its context?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q25/p1", "position": "Earlier recitation and invocation could suggest an audible prayer; this verse sets its volume.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī cites dawn recitation in 17:78 and listening in 17:107; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the command follows the naming dispute and the Prophet's audible invocation; al-Ālūsī says the basmala occasion especially suits the transition."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q26", "question": "What does 'your prayer' refer to in the voice command?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣalāt denotes recitation, supplication, testimony, or the act of prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q26/p1", "position": "Supplication and petition.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha, Mujāhid, ʿUrwa, Makḥūl and many others transmit this; Ibn ʿAbbās mentions people saying 'Have mercy on me' aloud. A Companion says public petitions for forgiveness disclose sins to mockers. Al-Rāzī relays the Prophetic warning and Ibn Masʿūd's criterion that a speaker should hear himself. Al-Suyūṭī notes the report can fit supplication within prayer."}, {"id": "17:110/q26/p2", "position": "Qurʾānic recitation within ritual prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ṭabarī connect it to Meccan recitation; al-Rāzī reasons that only prayer's spoken part can be loud or soft. Al-Qurṭubī calls this whole-for-part metonymy and cites 17:78 and the ḥadīth on al-Fātiḥa; al-Biqāʿī and al-Bursawī contrast the earlier use of dawn recitation for prayer. Al-Ālūsī includes basmala and other verses; most commentators, he says, prefer this explanation."}, {"id": "17:110/q26/p3", "position": "The outward and inward performance of worship: avoid showiness and neglect.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿAbbās forbid polished public display with corrupt private practice, ostentatious prayer, or abandonment from fear or embarrassment. ʿIkrima also warns against conspicuousness and excessive concealment. Qāshānī gives an inward extension: neither assert a separate self nor disappear so fully that others cannot follow; al-Bursawī's inward source favors public congregational obligations and private voluntary prayers."}, {"id": "17:110/q26/p4", "position": "The tashahhud within ritual prayer.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha and Ibn Sīrīn are reported to connect it with loud Bedouin tashahhud; al-Qurṭubī says Ibn Masʿūd treated concealment of tashahhud as Sunna, as transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir."}, {"id": "17:110/q26/p5", "position": "It covers both recitation and supplication in prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī includes Qurʾān, requests and remembrance in the same command. Ibn Ḥajar, reported by al-Suyūṭī, reconciles the two occasions by locating petition inside prayer, aided by Abū Hurayra's Kaʿba report. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows both early glosses, and Kur'an Yolu points to adjacent recitation, petition and the prayer of 17:111."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q27", "question": "What does 'tartīl' mean in associated recitation explanation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q27/p1", "position": "Clear measured articulation with separated letters.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares the articulated recitation to even or spaced teeth and gives ratl with kasra for a man with spaced teeth."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q28", "question": "What related prayer practice is warned against?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q28/p1", "position": "Staring toward the sky during prayer may imperil one's sight.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports Ibrāhīm's warning."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q29", "question": "What does 'tukhāfit' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q29/p1", "position": "To lower or weaken the voice, sometimes to inaudibility.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī extend khafata to death and withering crops; al-Thaʿlabī says a cooled corpse. {"id": "17:110/q30", "question": "What wider principle does the middle path teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q30/p1", "position": "Virtue lies between excessive extremes.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī adduces the middle community (2:143), balanced spending (25:67) and measured giving (17:29). {"id": "17:110/q31", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the two names and prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q31/p1", "position": "The names describe stations of annihilation; moderated prayer preserves abiding and guidance for others.", "reasons": "Qāshānī makes Allah the all-comprehensive essence and al-Raḥmān the mother attribute; al-Ālūsī expounds the Fuṭūḥāt's distinction between divine meaning and merciful-breath form, human utterances as translations, and realities behind letters. Al-Sulamī says true invocation rests on faith and al-Wāsiṭī says divine reality exceeds predicates. Al-Ālūsī cautions this is not simple petitionary duʿāʾ."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q32", "question": "How is this passage related to the sequence of sūras?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q32/p1", "position": "The order runs from the promised Praised Station to Muhammad's mission as mercy.", "reasons": "Elmalılı connects 17:79 with 21:107 and treats the intervening sūras as intentionally ordered."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q33", "question": "What protective effect is reported for reciting this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q33/p1", "position": "Reciting it before sleep protects a house from theft.", "reasons": "A report in al-Durr and al-Itqān tells of a thief unable to leave with belongings; al-Ālūsī notes a route through Nahshal and al-Ḍaḥḥāk whose excerpt is cut off, then gives the story of a migrant's protected house."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q34", "question": "What recitation practice is reported for this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q34/p1", "position": "The Prophet recited this sūra and al-Zumar nightly.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites ʿĀʾisha's report."}]}
{"id": "17:110/q35", "question": "How was this sūra valued among early revelations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "17:110/q35/p1", "position": "The Prophet called this and following sūras his earliest treasured possessions.", "reasons": "Elmalılı relays Ibn Masʿūd and glosses the saying as early Meccan revelation treasured in memory and devotion."}]}
{"id": "18:1/q01", "question": "Why does the verse open with praise of God?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause performs divine self-praise or instructs human praise; the accounts of revelation's benefit largely agree.", "positions": [{"id": "18:1/q01/p1", "position": "God is inherently worthy of praise and praises Himself for revelation, the supreme gift benefiting Muhammad especially and humanity generally.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā says God deserves praise; al-Māwardī and al-Baghawī distinguish the Prophet's special benefit from creation's general benefit.
